$comment: The economics of a Flock deployment: what the money buys, what it does not, how the price moved, who does the work, and how big the business is. Every row cites sources.json. Prices are per unit per year unless stated.

intro.headline: About $3,000 a year buys the whole thing, except the parts that go wrong
intro.summary: A city does not buy a camera. It leases one: hardware, pole, panel, cellular data, cloud, software and installation labour in one annual fee. The customer pays separately for installation itself, for permits and electricians, and for anything lost, stolen or damaged. The list price rose from $2,500 to $3,000 in January 2024 and the one-time install fee quietly moved from a few hundred dollars to over a thousand.

Bucket trucks, lane closures, MUTCD traffic control plans

Relocation $350 on an existing pole, $750 on a Flock pole, $5,000 on a DOT pole; technician visit $350

history.note: Greenville, SC: 11 cameras for $2,000 a year, no install fee, paid from asset forfeiture. A loss-leader, not a list price.
The settled market rate in council packets
Indio, CA told the increase was coming and offered $2,500 for a five-year term
Existing customers could hold $2,500 by signing five years: a price rise traded for term length
Greenville renewal, 50 cameras; the termination fee was $200 in 2019
Park Ridge, IL invoice; products renamed on 1 February 2025 so 'Falcon' becomes 'Flock Safety LPR' on paper
Flock's own published schedule; most secondary sources still repeat the old $250 figure

workflow.flock: Presents viable options and keeps final say on placement
workflow.customer: Approves the deployment plan; clears it with public works

workflow.flock: Proceeds on non-permit sites; historically a ten-location minimum for a partial install
workflow.customer: Signs; starts permit applications; gets an electrician quote for AC sites

workflow.flock: 'Assists in packaging your application'; has working relationships with some DOTs such as IDOT
workflow.customer: 'Solely responsible for any permits or associated costs, and managing the permitting process'
workflow.other: DOT, public works or pole owner issues the permit

workflow.flock: Technician checks solar exposure, sight line to the road and cellular signal; flags each spot
Coordinates the call; a ten-foot radius is marked
Standard MUTCD control by the technician
workflow.customer: Provides a patrol escort or pays for full traffic control; custom plans can double the cost

workflow.flock: Field Operations technician or an approved third-party technician sets the pole, panel and camera and aims it
workflow.customer: Pays for a bucket truck when the mount is above about 15 ft

workflow.flock: Supplies the kit; verifies power remotely while the electrician is on site
workflow.customer: Hires, pays and carries liability for the electrician; must finish within two days of install

workflow.flock: Checks capture quality for seven business days, then grants full access. The contract clock starts here.
Maintains its equipment; bills moves and non-defect replacements per the fee schedule
workflow.customer: Pays for relocations, losses, electrical faults and outage downtime

workforce.v: A Field Operations team of travelling technicians, organised in at least three regions, doing new installs and maintenance about half and half; postings list $55,000 to $65,000

The contract allows third-party labour and Flock's installer app is restricted to its technicians 'and approved third party technicians'; DISH's OnTech arm has been identified as one such installer, with no public split between in-house and contract work
Falcon Flex is customer-installed with no on-site service; its contract clock starts at signature rather than validation
Installs typically complete six to eight weeks after locations are final; permitting can add two months or more
Cameras assembled in Atlanta; a 97,000 square foot Smyrna, Georgia plant opened in 2025 for drones, panel assembly and refurbishing returned hardware

permitting.permit: Public works approval; sometimes an encroachment permit
permitting.who: Customer owns the process; Flock helps package it
Customer on paper; Flock works some DOTs directly
permitting.note: Hundreds of cameras went up without approval in Florida, Illinois and South Carolina; South Carolina found 200 or more and froze new installs in 2023. Florida revoked every state right-of-way permit on 31 August 2026 with 30 days to remove.

permitting.permit: Attachment agreement with the pole owner
permitting.note: One telecom company said cameras were placed on its poles without its knowledge

permitting.permit: Breakaway or MASH-rated pole where required
permitting.note: Reporting in 2026 found poles set inside clear zones without breakaway bases

permitting.permit: Owner consent; encroachment permit if the pole meets public right of way

permitting.note: Roanoke installed 30 of 41 Raven audio sensors at unapproved spots after a city data-entry error, then scrapped the program

contract.v: 'All Flock Hardware is owned exclusively by Flock'; the customer may not move, adjust or take possession of it, except self-installed Flex units
Older contracts promise removal within six months; the 2026 terms say 'a commercially reasonable time'. Verona, Evanston and Cambridge all found cameras up or reinstalled after cancelling
One, two, five and ten-year terms exist; renewals roll automatically unless notice is given 30 days before the end
Half the year's fee plus the install fee is due up front, a quarter when installation starts, the rest on completion
An outage of a day or more extends the term by the same length, pro rata; there is no cash credit

The 'Flock does not own and shall not sell Customer Data' sentence was deleted, the data licence became perpetual and product-improvement scoped, disputes moved to Georgia arbitration, the gross-negligence carve-out left the liability cap, and the non-appropriation exit was narrowed
OMNIA, Sourcewell, Texas DIR and similar contracts let cities skip competitive bidding; sole-source memos cite the network effect: 'all of our neighboring communities are in the Flock system'

scale.v: 120,000+ claimed in 49 states; about 96,000 independently mapped
5,000+ law-enforcement agencies and 6,000+ communities, plus retailers such as Home Depot and Lowe's whose lot cameras feed police searches
Annual recurring revenue about $500 million by March 2026, up from $285 million at the end of 2024
$7.5 billion in 2025, $8.4 billion in April 2026; roughly $1 billion raised

Texas directed at least $30 million in insurance-fee grants to local Flock networks before the governor halted it in August 2026; Florida approved grant funding for about 440 readers days before its DOT banned them from state roads
Direct, city by city, with police as advocates: a leaked guide coaches officers on presenting to councils; free pilots and grant-writing help lower the first-year cost

unknowns.v: Gross margin and bill-of-materials cost: Flock is private and no teardown has priced the parts
Field technician headcount and the split between employees and contractors
How many Florida right-of-way cameras came down by the 30 September 2026 deadline
